passage: I live next door to Jahnavi and Rafiq, a married couple, and the wall between us isn't thick. All I can tell you is what I heard and saw. Sunday after Rafiq's parents left, Jahnavi stood on the balcony alone for a long time. Later I heard voices. Jahnavi said, calmly, "When your parents criticise me and you agree with them, I feel alone in the house that is meant to be ours. I don't want you to stop seeing them. I want us to face this as a team." Rafiq answered something I couldn't catch. Then it went quiet. The next morning Jahnavi watered the plants, stood straight and nodded to me as usual. I honestly can't say whether the talk solved anything, or what Jahnavi felt behind that nod.

qa.q: What did Jahnavi do on the balcony after Rafiq's parents left?
qa.a: Jahnavi stood alone for a long time.

qa.q: What does Jahnavi say about how it feels when Rafiq agrees with the parents' criticism?
qa.a: That Jahnavi feels alone in the house that is meant to be theirs.

qa.q: What does Jahnavi ask for, and why is it a fair way to raise the issue?
qa.a: Jahnavi asks that they face the issue as a team, and says clearly that Jahnavi does not want Rafiq to stop seeing the parents, so the request is about dignity and not about cutting ties.

qa.q: How might Rafiq have felt hearing Jahnavi ask to face it as a team?
qa.a: Rafiq may have felt caught between Jahnavi and the parents, or relieved that Jahnavi did not want the visits to stop. The quiet afterwards and the calm morning hint that the words were taken in, though the neighbour cannot be sure.

grounding: Shows a partner repeatedly taking their parents' side, the protagonist feeling alone at home, saying what they need and asking to face it as a team without demanding cut ties, seen by an observer.

passage:
Anirban,

I'm writing this because when I try to say it out loud, we end up arguing about who said what.

Since your parents moved in, three things keep happening. Your mother changes how I've arranged the kitchen, your father comments on how late I work, and when I object, you tell me they mean well. Last Sunday, in front of your aunt, you agreed that I "take everything personally". I went to the bathroom and cried. I'm your wife, Anirban, not a lodger.

I am not asking you to choose between them and me. I would never ask you to push your parents away. They're your family and I want them in our life.

What I need is to feel we're a team in our own home. Can we sit down, just the two of us, and decide together what to say to them about the kitchen and my hours? I miss feeling you're on my side.

Dolma

qa.q: What did Anirban agree with in front of his aunt?
qa.a: Anirban agreed that Dolma "takes everything personally".

qa.q: What does Dolma feel in her own home?
qa.a: Dolma feels alone and hurt, as if her husband is not on her side, and she cried after the Sunday remark.

qa.q: How does Dolma's email help them face the problem as a team?
qa.a: It names specific things, asks for a private talk to decide together, and makes clear she is not asking him to cut ties with his parents.

qa.q: How might Anirban feel reading Dolma's email?
qa.a: He might feel defensive at first, but her calm tone and her respect for his parents may help him see how lonely she has been.

grounding: An email shows a woman whose partner keeps siding with his parents, saying what she needs and asking to face it as a team without asking him to cut ties.

passage:
Salma, you asked why I've been so quiet at work. Okay. I'm Indu, your oldest friend, and I'll tell you properly.

Last month Arvind's mother told a room full of guests that her daughter-in-law's job at the bank means I've "abandoned the home". And Arvind laughed. Then later, alone, he said, "She's old, don't fight her." It happened again at his cousin's naming ceremony. I stood in my own house feeling like a visitor.

So on Tuesday I asked him to sit with me, no phones. I said, "When your mother criticises me and you laugh, I feel completely alone. I don't want you to stop seeing her. I want us to handle her comments together." He went quiet for a long time. Then he said he hadn't noticed he always laughed.

We've agreed he'll speak up next time. Nothing has changed yet. But for the first time in months, I feel a little less alone.

qa.q: What did Arvind's mother say about Indu's job?
qa.a: She said Indu's job at the bank meant she had "abandoned the home".

qa.q: How did Indu feel when Arvind laughed?
qa.a: Indu felt completely alone and like a visitor in her own house.

qa.q: What would you advise Indu to do if Arvind forgets his promise?
qa.a: Calmly remind him of their agreement in private, and keep asking to handle it as a team rather than demanding he cut off his mother.

qa.q: How does Arvind seem to experience the Tuesday talk?
qa.a: Arvind seems surprised and thoughtful, going quiet and admitting he hadn't noticed he always laughed.

grounding: A spoken account shows a woman whose partner sides with his parent against her, stating her needs and asking to work as a team without demanding he cut ties.
